Standard list-based tab managers and even grouped extensions often fail when you need to map out complex, decentralized information architectures. The desire for a spatial, infinite-canvas view—like Excalidraw—is a much better mental model for high-density research and development.

The core technical hurdle here is the "cache and context" requirement. If you just extract the URLs to a graph tool, you lose the DOM state, the back/forward history, and the active session data. You need a solution that manages the living tabs rather than just scraping their addresses.

Here are a few ways to achieve a hierarchical, graph-based tab interface without losing your active session states.

1. The Custom Local Graph UI (Remote Control Approach)

Since you are looking for an Excalidraw-like infinityboard but need the tabs to act as functional buttons, the most robust solution is to build a decoupled local interface that acts as a "remote control" for your browser.

You can write a lightweight Chrome/Firefox extension that does only two things:

  1. Broadcasts Tab IDs: The extension reads your open tabs and sends their metadata (Title, URL, Favicon, and native tabId) via a local WebSocket to a custom frontend.
  2. Listens for Clicks: When you click a node in your custom UI, it sends a message back to the extension to execute chrome.tabs.update(tabId, {active: true}) and chrome.windows.update(windowId, {focused: true}).

For the visual layer, you can use a library like React Flow. It provides a node-based, infinite-canvas graph topology out of the box. You can map out your hierarchical substructures, and because it's just a local web app, every node can be a clickable button that instantly surfaces the exact, fully-cached tab in your browser.

Handling Memory: To prevent hundreds of tabs from crashing your machine, your extension can utilize chrome.tabs.discard(tabId). This unloads the tab from memory but keeps it fully intact in the browser's tab strip (preserving the back/forward cache and session context) until you click its corresponding node in your graph to wake it up.

2. TabFS (Tabs as Local Files)

If you prefer manipulating data via local-first environments, TabFS is a fascinating open-source project that mounts your browser tabs as a native file system on your OS.

  • Every open tab becomes a folder (e.g., fs/tabs/by-id/123/).
  • Inside that folder are files representing the tab's state: url.txt, title.txt, and even text.txt (the scraped DOM).
  • You can close or focus a tab by interacting with these local files (e.g., deleting a folder closes the tab).

By bringing your active browser state into a local directory structure, you can easily pipe this data into a local Markdown graph topology or script a custom metadata index that visualizes the hierarchical layout you want.

3. Out-of-the-box Hierarchical Alternatives

If you want to test existing tools before building a custom pipeline:

  • BrainTool: It operates as a separate window and uses plain text (Org-mode syntax) to build a deeply hierarchical tree of your tabs. It allows you to open, close, and group tabs based on a structured hierarchy, though it relies on an outliner UI rather than a 2D spatial graph.
  • Tree Style Tab (Firefox) + Auto Tab Discard: While strictly vertical rather than a decentralized graph, Tree Style Tab allows for infinite nesting (parent/child substructures). Paired with a discard extension, it safely freezes the tabs while preserving their structural relationship and context.

Embedding Excalidraw as an interactive command center is completely achievable. You don't have to build the canvas from scratch—Excalidraw is open-source and exports a standard React component (@excalidraw/excalidraw). This means you can mount a fully functional, infinite whiteboard directly inside a local extension page and move that tab to a second monitor.

Here is how you can architect a lightweight, decentralized system.

Firefox vs. Chrome

For a heavy-duty tab manager, Firefox is the better choice.

Chrome's Manifest V3 architecture aggressively suspends background service workers after short periods of inactivity. If your background script is tracking active tabs and maintaining complex graph states, Chrome will repeatedly kill the worker, forcing you to constantly write to and rehydrate from local storage. Firefox is much more forgiving with background memory, making it far more stable for an intensive, always-on visual manager.

The Architecture

Building the core state manager in Rust is an excellent route. You can design it exactly like a decoupled metadata index for local Markdown files, where the Rust backend maintains the graph topology of your tabs completely independently of the visual layer. The Excalidraw interface simply visualizes that index.

Here is how the pieces fit together:

1. The Rust & WebAssembly Core (The Index) The Rust module (compiled via wasm-pack) acts as the state manager. It intercepts the browser's native tab events (created, updated, closed) and maintains the hierarchical substructure. When you middle-click a link to open a new tab, Rust registers the "parent-child" relationship. It calculates where that new tab should live on the 2D plane (its X/Y coordinates) relative to its parent, ensuring the decentralized graph remains readable without nodes overlapping.

2. The Excalidraw Frontend (The Canvas) Your extension page runs React. You drop the <Excalidraw/> component into this page. The frontend receives the graph topology from the Rust core as a JSON payload. It then programmatically generates rectangles, text labels (for the tab titles), and connecting lines on the canvas. Excalidraw allows you to attach hidden customData to elements, so you embed the native browser tabId directly inside the shape's data payload.

3. The JavaScript Bridge (The Interactivity) When you pan around your Excalidraw window and click on a tab node, a JavaScript onChange or onPointerDown listener detects the selection. The script reads the hidden tabId from the selected shape and executes a standard WebExtensions API call: browser.tabs.update(tabId, {active: true}).

The target tab instantly focuses in your main window, preserving all of your cache, back/forward history, and living DOM state. By keeping the Excalidraw UI as a lightweight visualizer and treating your Rust backend as the authoritative index, you get a highly resilient, spatial manager without sacrificing native browser performance.
